paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Delta County, Texas, was a campaign in the summer of 1895 in which notices posted by bands the press called "White Caps" ordered every Black resident of the county to leave or be hanged. Black families abandoned farms and standing crops, and a farmer named William Stephens, who stayed past his notice, was reported shot dead at his door, though a local merchant said he knew of no killing. The movement spread into neighboring Lamar County, where a Black church was burned, and the story ran in white papers across the country.

According to a dispatch from Paris, in adjoining Lamar County, one night in the week before August 5 every Black resident of Delta County was notified to leave at once or "be taken out and hanged." Other notices warned that white men who protected them would meet the same fate.

The notices set off what the dispatch called "a perfect stampede," although, it said, "the good citizens" offered the Black residents protection. Within five miles, 2,000 acres were abandoned with the crops in the field and contracts for the next year canceled, while a few Black landowners stayed behind to sell their farms for whatever they could get.

William Stephens, who lived near Pacio, did not leave when his ten days' notice expired, because fleeing would have cost him his growing crop. According to his mother, who reached Paris on August 12, he was called to his door about four o'clock on Saturday morning and shot down by the White Caps in front of his family. A notice was posted within thirty yards of his house, and his brother had fled to Paris.
By then notices had appeared near Glory in Lamar County, a Black church there was burned on a Thursday night, and Black residents of Paris were told to leave on peril of their lives.

Black residents of Delta County published an appeal "To the citizens of Lamar county," calling themselves "the poorest and most worthless people in the State of Texas," denying any crime and asking for protection. The August 12 dispatch said officers were pursuing the perpetrators and that three unnamed people had been arrested.

At an inquest at Glory on August 13 into the burning of the Edora church, witnesses said a man named Hinson had come from Delta County to organize young farm hands. One witness, Will Sheppard, fled after his dictated handwriting nearly matched the notices, and George Kitchen confessed that the group had burned the church and printed the notices. The jury blamed the three men, Kitchen was held and a warrant issued for Hinson.
No report of an arrest, inquest or trial for the killing of William Stephens appears in the coverage.

Two Paris wire dispatches carried the story. The first ran on August 6 under headlines such as "NEGROES DRIVEN OUT" in the San Francisco Call, "OUTLAWRY IN TEXAS" in a Virginia paper and "KU KLUX IN DELTA COUNTY, TEX." in the New York Sun. Shortened versions reached the Providence News, Vermont's Middlebury Register and the Chicago Eagle.

The second, with the mother's account and the appeal, ran on August 13 as "SHOT BY WHITE CAPS" in the Indianapolis Journal and "WHITE CAP CARMIYAL [Carnival]" in a Kentucky Evening Bulletin. Both dispatches cast white Texans as opposed to the bands, saying the lawlessness was "not countenanced by the whites generally," and a Paris paper urged citizens to "pump lead into every White Cap found posting notices or doing other unlawful acts."

The Sacramento Record-Union called for federal intervention, writing that "a state of anarchy prevails in Delta County," and later hoped officers would "hang a group of the rascally bulldozers." Weekly news digests cut the episode to single lines, the Kanabec County Times reporting that one man who refused to go "was shot dead." Every report found was in white papers; no Black-press account was found.

The killing rested on the mother's account, and the same dispatch quoted Joseph Price, a merchant near Glory several miles away, as saying that so far as he knew no Black person had been shot by White Caps; it concluded, "Reports are conflicting." The Record-Union's August 15 editorial, unlike the dispatches, said the notices threatened whipping or murder, added that several Black men were flogged and placed the shooting on the day of the church burning.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Delta County, Texas
bases: Notices ordered every Black resident of Delta County to leave under threat of hanging and the exodus was called complete (A1, A12); the one reported killing was of a man who refused to go (A13, A22).

Separate Paris dispatches of Aug. 5 and Aug. 12 and the Glory inquest report all describe the notices and the flight of Black residents from Delta County (A1, A12, A18); the killing of William Stephens rests on his mother's account and was denied by a merchant (A13).

accounts.label: Paris wire, Aug. 5
accounts.gist: Every Black resident of Delta County was notified to leave or be hanged; a stampede followed despite offers of protection by 'good citizens', leaving 2,000 acres abandoned.

accounts.label: Victim's mother (Paris wire, Aug. 12)
accounts.gist: Her son William Stephens was called to his door at 4 a.m. Saturday and shot by White Caps after his ten days' notice expired.

accounts.label: Merchant Joseph Price
accounts.gist: So far as he knew, no Black person had been shot or murdered by White Caps.

accounts.label: Delta County Black residents' appeal
accounts.gist: They denied any crime, asked white people of Lamar County to protect them and said they were unable to go anywhere.

accounts.label: Glory inquest testimony
accounts.gist: Hinson from Delta County organized local farm hands; Kitchen confessed to burning the Edora church and printing notices; the jury found three whitecaps responsible.

accounts.label: Sacramento Record-Union editorial
accounts.gist: Notices threatened whipping or murder; a man was shot from ambush, a church burned and several Black men flogged, all organized by a man from Delta County.

framing.detail: The Aug. 5 dispatch ran under 'NEGROES DRIVEN OUT', 'OUTLAWRY IN TEXAS' and 'KU KLUX IN DELTA COUNTY, TEX.', stressing the 'outrage' and the protection offered by 'good citizens'.
The Aug. 12 dispatch said the lawlessness was 'not countenanced by the whites generally' and quoted a Paris paper urging citizens to 'pump lead into every White Cap'.
Sacramento Record-Union editorials called Delta County anarchic, urged federal intervention and hoped officers would hang the 'rascally bulldozers'.
Weekly news digests reduced it to one-line items about notices, abandoned acres and one man 'shot dead'.

versions.value: William Stephens shot dead by White Caps (mother's account)
No Black person shot or murdered by White Caps, to the knowledge of merchant Joseph Price

conflicts.note: Price lived near Glory, several miles from the scene; the mother claimed direct knowledge. Later digests and the Record-Union treated the killing as fact (A19, A22).

versions.value: Notices threatened whipping or murder; several Black men flogged

conflicts.note: The floggings appear only in the Sacramento editorial and may refer to the Glory section of Lamar County.

versions.value: Church burned Thursday night; Stephens shot Saturday morning
Shooting and church burning on the same day

conflicts.note: The Paris dispatches are closer to the events than the Sacramento editorial.
